fragments.text: Good morning. Good afternoon or good evening depending on when and where you're viewing this from. My name is Yasmin Abu Lubben and I'm a professor of political science at the University of Alberta in Canada and I also hold the Canada Research Chair and the Politics of Citizenship and Human Rights. I'd like to thank Cordell Greene, the UNESCO Information for All Program, and the organizers of the fifth Artificial Intelligence for Information Accessibility Conference for the very kind invitation to speak. Today AI is one of those areas that's really prone to either utopian or dystopian prophecies about our future and this might not be all that different from what's happened historically when you've had different innovations and inventions that powerfully

In fact actually AI has been around for many years but our public awareness of it is changing and it is precisely at these moments that it's really important to have conversations and research that allow for careful examination and this is a big reason why I really welcome the kind of discussions that the conference allows for. So in my talk today I want to discuss

fragments.text: the implications of artificial intelligence for human migration and what I argue is that we really need to be aware whether as policymakers or as researchers or as global citizens we need to be aware of the challenges and concerns AI carries in relation to migration from a human rights perspective. It's this awareness that can potentiate our ability to shape a collective discussion and future that centers humans and their needs. So I'm going to proceed in three parts. The first is to provide some brief overview of global migration today. This is followed secondly by a discussion of how AI may potentially be of benefit and then finally I'll address where AI is of concern.

fragments.text: So let me turn to the first part of my talk and just say something about migration. You know sometimes in the news we hear migration talked about as a crisis or as a problem but in actuality the position I would advance is that it is normal. I say it's normal because people have always traversed across humanly created boundaries and barriers and people are still on the move today. The global estimate by the international organization for migration is that there are some 281 million people living in a country other than the one that they were born in which is actually about three times the estimated number if you go back to 1970. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees notes that today there are 117 million people that are forcibly displaced and of these some 37.6 million would be defined as refugees by the definition used by the UN Convention on Refugees. The 1951 UN Convention on Refugees defines a refugee as someone who is forced to flee their country for reasons of a well-founded fear of persecution. So I highlight the reality of refugees because many states around the world have agreed to the UN Refugee Convention in related protocol and therefore have a special responsibility to not return refugees to situations of danger. fragments.text: future, considering the challenges and the opportunities presented by AI and immigration, I think we need a balanced assessment. Potentially AI can carry benefits, but so too, there are also risks. And I join others in emphasizing the need for more public awareness and discussion of technology and surveillance. I also think there need to be stronger legislative frameworks, which can give assurance that there is regular monitoring and safeguards against bias as well as accountability and oversight. Across societies and globally, there are new discussions we can and need to be having to better mitigate the problematic possibilities that detract from human rights centered migration.
